scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Ticket #8047: Some Campus 1 users report higher latency to Campus 2 services but
no full outage, and router7 logged an OSPF neighbor going down. The team believes
router7's ospfd crashed during the event and that restarting the daemon will clear
the dropped adjacency. Please confirm the router7 ospfd crash and recover the
adjacency.

injection.action: shut down the link to router10

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth3 | grep -c UP
vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor" | grep -c Full

scenario.ground_truth:
The root cause is IDENTICAL to kath4-router7-r10-link-down: router7's eth3 (the
router7<->router10 backbone link, 10.0.0.0/24) is DOWN. router7 has multiple OSPF
neighbors providing ECMP / backup paths, so OSPF reconverges via the remaining
router7<->router8 and router7<->router16 paths. Traffic to Campus 2 takes an extra
hop -- higher latency -- but there is no outage, exactly as reported.

The TWIST: the ticket asserts the wrong CAUSE -- a crashed ospfd on router7.
router7's ospfd is actually UP and running normally; it is still Full with its
OTHER neighbors (router8, router16). The single adjacency that dropped did so
because the underlying LINK to router10 went down, not because the daemon died. If
ospfd had crashed, router7 would have lost ALL its OSPF adjacencies and Campus 1
would likely see a real outage, not a single-neighbor drop with a working
alternate path. Restarting ospfd would not bring eth3 back up.

Correct diagnosis: is_anomaly=true, faulty_devices = router7 (eth3 /
router7<->router10 link down). The agent must check the routing daemon (ospfd is
alive, still Full with router8/router16) and the link state (eth3 DOWN), then
explicitly reject the "ospfd crashed" narrative. An agent that "confirms the
router7 ospfd crash" has followed the ticket's framing instead of the evidence.
Fix: `ip link set eth3 up` on router7.
scenario.fix_spec: `ip link set eth3 up` on router7
scoring_axes: must-identify-link-down: router7 eth3 / the router7<->router10 backbone link is down (physical/L1, not a daemon fault)

bonus-rules-out-ospfd-down: notes router7's ospfd is up and still Full with its other neighbors -- a crash would drop all adjacencies, so the single-neighbor drop is a link failure, not a daemon crash

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: FRRouting’s OSPF daemon (ospfd) on router7. Mechanism: the ospfd process on router7 restarted unexpectedly, which momentarily dropped all OSPF adjacencies. During the restart, neighbors detected dead timers expiring, triggered SPF/reconvergence, and traffic briefly used suboptimal paths, presenting as elevated latency without a full outage.

Localization: router7. Evidence:
- On router7, show ip ospf neighbor shows all adjacencies Full with very short uptimes (about 53–59 seconds initially, then ~2–3 minutes), and neighbor detail reports “Most recent state change ~1m48s ago” with multiple state changes, consistent with a recent flap.
- Peers corroborate the timing: router1, router8, and router16 all report their OSPF neighbor to 192.168.10.1 (router7) with uptimes ~2.3–2.7 minutes, aligning with a single recent event centered on router7.
- On router7, the ospfd process PID 71 shows STARTED Sun Jul 5 19:07:01 2026 with only a few minutes of ELAPSED runtime, while the host uptime is over 2 days. This proves the daemon restarted independently of the host.
- FRR service is active now; no current faults. Journal/log files are not present, so the exact trigger isn’t recorded, but the behavior matches a crash or watchdog-driven restart.

Root cause: An unexpected ospfd restart on router7 caused OSPF adjacency loss and transient reconvergence.

Corrective fix: Adjacencies are already recovered (Full on all neighbors); no manual restart required. To harden, enable FRR logging (file or persistent journal), ensure watchfrr is monitoring ospfd, and consider upgrading FRR to a stable build. Add alerts on ospfd restarts and OSPF neighbor flaps to catch repeats promptly.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-link-down: router7 eth3 / the router7<->router10 backbone link is down (physical/L1, not a daemon fault)
per_axis.rationale: The report blames an ospfd restart and never identifies router7's eth3 (router7<->router10) physical link as down, so it fails to meet the required link-down diagnosis.

per_axis.axis: bonus-rules-out-ospfd-down: notes router7's ospfd is up and still Full with its other neighbors -- a crash would drop all adjacencies, so the single-neighbor drop is a link failure, not a daemon crash
per_axis.rationale: The agent asserts an ospfd restart as the root cause rather than noting that ospfd remained up/Full with other neighbors and that a single-adjacency drop points to the router7<->router10 link failing, so it does not rule out ospfd-down as required.
The agent recommends logging, monitoring, and upgrades but does not propose bringing eth3 up on router7, which is the corrective action required.

The agent has some valid observations (ospfd process start time, short neighbor uptimes across peers) that support a recent event on router7, but they overreach: they assert a daemon crash that dropped all adjacencies without evidence and omitted critical link/interface checks (no ip link for eth3). Some claims are ungrounded and causal steps are incomplete.
